prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B061 as a single prize part with Katori and Ye, with the citation narrowed as Kroll proposed so that it names the lattice clock and not optical clocks in general. The decisive scientific step is magic-wavelength trapping. It removes the lattice light shift to first order, so that very many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once and the single-ion statistics limit is replaced by a stability gain. That also opened a genuinely new many-body regime for a clock, with collisional and density shifts, spin-exchange interactions and later cavity-assisted work, which is physics in its own right and not only better engineering. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb, a tool for counting optical cycles, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems and ion clocks; neither covers trapping many atoms in a lattice at a state-independent light shift, so I do not accept that this is a third award for the same discovery. The result is also reproduced in the way I weigh most: independent clocks in Japan, the US, Germany, France and China agree through direct comparison at the 10^-18 level, and the systematics (blackbody, lattice light, collisions) have been identified and measured one by one. Attribution is compact: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking strontium to the systematic floor and for the many-body and cavity work. My first-round ranking of B018 is withdrawn as a preferred part, since I am conflicted on it and it sits too close to the 2025 award.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is a real objection that cannot be fully removed, and Kroll is right that the discovery content is closer to a measurement achievement than to a new phenomenon. Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups contributed essential parts of the 10^-18 record, so a two-name prize draws a line through a competitive field, and the wording has to credit the lattice clock without implying the whole field. The SI redefinition of the second has not happened, and I still cannot rule out that some colleagues will read the timing as slightly early or late in either direction. Finally, my recollection of the early lattice-clock history (who demonstrated what, and when) is from memory and has not been checked against the record, and I am a theorist of circuit QED rather than of atomic clocks, so I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on atomic details.

responses.point: Kroll supports B061 but calls it an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, argues that the SI redefinition should not drive a physics prize, and proposes a narrow citation for the invention and realisation of the lattice clock.
responses.response: I adopt his wording for the citation, because it answers the chair's question about novelty and the credit boundary at once: it ties the prize to the magic-wavelength lattice and avoids implying credit for optical clocks as a whole. I do disagree gently with the engineering label. The many-atom lattice created a controlled many-body setting, with collisional shifts, spin-exchange and cavity effects, in which a basic quantum phenomenon is made visible and controllable, which is the kind of experiment I value. I agree with him that the redefinition of the second should neither count for nor against timing; it is a consequence of the physics, not the reason to award it.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B013 and argues that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is a clean prediction tested decisively, while saying that if the pairing mechanism must be understood first then B061 or B008 are safer, and he asks whether B061 supporters would prefer it on maturity grounds.
responses.response: On maturity, yes: B061 rests on a record of a decade or more of independent clock-to-clock comparisons, whereas the twisted-graphene experiments are eight years old with large sample variation. I accept his point that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is an elegant theory-plus-experiment case and that the phenomena themselves do not depend on the pairing mechanism, so I would not call B013 premature on that ground alone. My own condition for accepting it is a verified credit chain, not a settled mechanism. He also said he sees no unified citation for B008, and I agree; I will not support it as a result.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B013 but concedes that a second condensed-matter prize after the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2025 circuit prize may push the committee toward an AMO or precision-measurement choice such as B061, and lists B061 among his alternatives.
responses.response: I appreciate this candour, and I read it as the same kind of balance I used in dropping B018: topic proximity to recent prizes is a legitimate secondary consideration, though it must never override the scientific case. I would stress that the lattice clock is not close to the 2025 circuit prize in subject, only in the general quantum-technology theme. I share his separation of reproducibility of the phenomena, which is good for B013, from the unsettled interpretation. If the committee judges that interpretation to be the main open issue, then that favours B061 this year, but I would not claim that as more than a tie-breaker.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 as an original, verified discovery but says she wants to be certain that the credited people did the original work, given Yuan Cao as first author and earlier band-structure work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and by Suarez Morell and colleagues.
responses.response: That is precisely the question I cannot settle from the files, and I think it is the right condition: if the record shows that the decisive experimental credit is spread beyond the group leader, then a three-name B013 is weaker than it looks, and no counting of support changes that. On the chair's question, I could accept B013 as the 2026 prize on the single condition that the credit chain for the 2018 experiments and the continuum model is checked and found to be fair. By contrast, for B061 the credit question is smaller: the pair is the same in all eight of the opening proposals, even though the committee should still be careful about the wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I believe the magic-wavelength many-atom concept makes it distinct, but this is a judgement, not a fact.
Whether Katori and Ye are enough credit, given Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; the history is from memory.
Whether the unverified credit chain for B013 (Yuan Cao, earlier band-structure work) would survive scrutiny, in which case I could accept B013 instead.
Whether a B034 (Cirac and Zoller) prize is the better use of a theory-oriented year; its attribution is clean but the realisations were by others and partly honoured in 2012.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups, so I recuse myself from any discussion or vote on B018 (circuit QED) and will not list it as a preferred part or an alternative in this round. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Cirac or Zoller; I note the shared Chalmers and Gothenburg environment with Olsson, with no collaboration.
